old_title: Ukraine-Russia war latest: Moscow could attack a Nato country, warns Denmark
new_title: Ukraine-Russia live: Putin says peace 'on the table' - yet warns of further strikes

There is "a low but growing risk" that Russia would launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries that border it, Denmark intelligence has warned
Such attacks could include isolated strikes with long-range weapons like drones or missiles on infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or false-flag operations using Ukrainian-made drones, intelligence service chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said at a press conference.
He said Russia could also deploy a limited number of troops into a NATO border area, potentially under the pretext of protecting Russian minorities.
"The aim is not to take over the country, but to divide NATO," he said.
Meanwhile, Donald Trump is facing backlash after inviting Russian president Vladimir Putin to a December G20 meeting in Miami, for what would be his second US visit since the war began.
"It's clearly, I think, the wrong path to normalise people who are starting wars, who are going against the UN charter, who are killing and giving orders to kill civilians," said the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, speaking to Sky News.
Russia has invited Kim Jong Un to visit the country, the Tass news agency said
Russia has extended an official invitation to visit the country to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, a deputy foreign minister has said according to the TASS state news agency.
Moscow and Pyongyang have drawn markedly closer in recent years, with North Korea sending troops to fight alongside Russian forces in Ukraine in 2024 and deepening military cooperation under a mutual defence pact.
US and Indian top diplomats discuss Russia sanctions bill signed by Trump
US secretary of state Marco Rubio and Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar discussed on Wednesday US measures that could be leveled against countries that engage economically with Russia and Iran.
Last week, Trump signed the bill called "Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," named after deceased South Carolina Republican US Senator Lindsey Graham.
Rubio and Jaishankar "discussed sanctions that could be leveled against states that engage economically with Russia and Iran," the State Department said in a statement after their meeting in New York.
Jaishankar wrote on X he "reiterated India's interests and concerns with regard to SRIA."
India has previously told Washington that new measures to levy tariffs over the purchase of Russian oil could impact bilateral ties.
Don't weaken sanctions on Russian oligarchs, Zelensky pleads with world leaders - ICYMI
'Low but growing risk" that Russia would launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries, Denmark warns
Russia is likely to intensify its hybrid war against the West in the coming months, Denmark's defence intelligence service said in a new threat assessment on Thursday.
Hybrid warfare and sabotage on European soil gained renewed attention after Germany recently blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle Airport, prompting European Union members to call for new sanctions against Russia.
Moscow has repeatedly denied any involvement in hybrid warfare, sabotage operations in NATO countries, or plotting any confrontation.
The Russian embassy in Denmark rejected the assessment as unsupported by credible evidence and accused the West, led by Denmark, of driving up tensions over Ukraine.
"Our persistent warnings about the destructiveness of such an approach are being ignored," the embassy said in a written statement.
The defence intelligence service said Russia would carry out more frequent attacks against the West and NATO "with greater consequences for the countries targeted than in the past".
It added that there was "a low but growing risk" that Russia would launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries that border it.
"A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia's part and, like the intensified hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months," it said.
Such attacks could include isolated strikes with long-range weapons like drones or missiles on infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or false-flag operations using Ukrainian-made drones, intelligence service chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said at a press conference.
He said Russia could also deploy a limited number of troops into a NATO border area, potentially under the pretext of protecting Russian minorities.
Finnish leader pleads with Musk to help Ukraine hit Russian missile launchers
Alexander Stubb said on Thursday he pleaded with SpaceX owner Elon Musk to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage for Ukraine so it can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers located inside Russian territory.
With winter looming, Ukraine has an acute shortage of air defenses to repel Russian ballistic missiles, and Kyiv officials believe that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target the Russian launchers that fire the missiles.
"That's why ... I plead that Elon Musk would give the Ukrainians the possibility to use Starlink in areas where there are ballistic missile launchers, either in the occupied territory of Ukraine or in Russia for strategic purposes because that would save lives," Stubb said.
The Finnish leader, a staunch ally of Ukraine who also has good relations with US President Donald Trump, made the remark in an interview with Reuters in New York where world leaders have converged for the annual gathering at the United Nations.
President Volodymyr Zelensky used the event to press hard for ceasefires that would cover strikes on targets related to energy infrastructure and vessels in the Black Sea. Russia has given no public indication it wants to see such arrangements.
German minister calls for ceasefire starting around the Black Sea
German foreign minister Johann Wadephul has called for a full and immediate ceasefire in Ukraine, starting in the Black Sea, to safeguard grain and food supplies.
"Ukraine had a very good grain harvest this year. But because of the Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports, it can't be delivered to the world.
"Russia is thereby exacerbating hunger and starvation worldwide," he said in a statement published on Thursday.
Poland suspects Russia behind fire at Starlink satellite station
A fire broke out on Wednesday evening at a ground-based Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland providing connectivity for the region, including Ukraine, deputy prime minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said.
He added that the systems were now operational.
Poland has been on heightened alert for acts of sabotage since Russia's invasion of neighbouring Ukraine in 2022. Russia has repeatedly denied any such action.
"The fire engulfed the power station and the generator; it is clear that this act of sabotage was deliberately designed to disable the station - effectively cutting off the internet connection... and disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian military," he said.
"While everything is operational today, we must recognise -as Prime Minister Tusk recently noted - that this is an element of hybrid warfare."
He added that while it was not established that Russia was responsible for the fire, "many signs suggest this aligns with Russia's new doctrine of attack".
Zelensky tells world leaders that Putin is 'patient zero' for spreading war globally - but Ukraine has a cure
Volodymyr Zelensky looked tired. His delivery was halting. Like the country he leads he can barely comprehend that he is still talking of war into the fifth year of Ukraine's defence against Russia.
He has a new message and a new way to deliver it. Vladimir Putin, he told the assembled world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, is "patient zero" spreading the infection of war to Africa, Asia, all over the world.
"Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory, attack another country instead of simply stopping and running his own country, the Ukrainian president said.
Zelensky signs drone deals with Finland, Australia and other countries
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky says he has signed a "drone deal" with Finland, another in a series of agreements combining Kyiv's technical expertise with other countries' industrial capacity.
"We are always ready to share what has helped us save lives with our closest friends," Mr Zelensky wrote.
When the war began in February 2022, Ukraine had limited experience in drone technology. Kyiv has rapidly developed its expertise and is now able to down drones, many of them designed by Iran.
It has offered its technology to a wide range of countries, many of them in the Middle East, facing Iranian weaponry.
Kyiv has now clinched "drone deals" with 10 countries and has an accord with the European Union.
In his address to the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, Zelensky said a security accord had also been concluded with Australia.
He described the drone deals as "ready-made security formats that we adapt to each specific country and each specific region".
"We are already working with partners in the Gulf, the South Caucasus, and across Europe through drone deals."
Developing drones, he said, allowed countries to control borders, mountain areas and roads "and without them, this would simply be impossible".

Russian president Vladimir Putin has said all proposals for a settlement to the war in Ukraine remain "on the table," but has warned Kyiv to prepare for a sustained wave of retaliatory strikes.
Addressing journalists in St. Petersburg on Friday, the Russian leader claimed Moscow was ready to resume peace negotiations after his party secured a record supermajority Russia's parliamentary elections this week.
However, Putin accused Ukrainian forces of intentionally derailing potential diplomatic channels with long-range drone strikes on polling stations during the voting period.
Dismissing Kyiv's recent military operations, Putin said: "They are the ones who started it... Everywhere, on every front. Are these playthings, child's play?
"[Ukraine] should therefore be made to feel Russia's retaliatory strikes and understand that no provocative actions ... will work. They're only making things worse for themselves."
While insisting that ceasefire frameworks and diplomatic solutions remain possible, Putin stressed that Moscow will first carefully assess what best serves its own national interests before agreeing to any terms.
The comments come as Ukraine's president Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed in Washington that he asked US president Donald Trump to press Chinese President Xi Jinping to use Beijing's leverage over Moscow.
Four dead in Russian strikes across Ukraine
Russian attacks killed four people across Ukraine on Saturday, officials said, as the aerial war between Moscow and Kyiv intensified.
Russia has hammered Ukraine with cruise and ballistic missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones in recent weeks while front line progress has slowed.
Two women in Zaporizhzhia died when they were trapped beneath the rubble of their destroyed home, Zaporizhzhia's regional military administration said. A separate Russian attack on the city of Sumy also killed two people, local officials said.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, two people were injured in the Kyiv region overnight after a Russian drone attack caused a fire at a warehouse in the Boryspil district. Russian drones also hit several districts in the Ukrainian capital itself, injuring four and damaging residential and office buildings, officials said.
Russia's defence ministry said on Saturday that its attack on Kyiv had damaged a data centre that supported both cellphone internet services and Starlink satellite communication systems.
Putin discusses energy cooperation with Serbian president
Russian president Vladimir Putin discussed the Ukraine war and energy cooperation with Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic during a phone call, the Kremlin said on Saturday.
Vucic has described Serbia as "neutral" when it comes to the Ukraine conflict. The country has long held close relations with Russia but has also supported UN resolutions condemning Putin's aggression.
Three killed in Ukrainian attack on Krasnodar region, says Russia
Three people were killed and two injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's Krasnodar region, local authorities there have said.
A local task force said fires at industrial sites that had broken out as a result of the attack had been extinguished.
Zelensky says he got Trump's OK for Patriot licences
The Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky says Donald Trump confirmed this week that he had made a final decision to allow Kyiv to get licences to produce Patriot air defence systems.
Ukraine is desperate for more of the American-made air defence systems that are needed to stop Russia's ballistic missiles, but they have been in short supply since the war in Iran started on 28 February.
Trump had said in July that he would allow Ukraine to make its own Patriots but later appeared to be reconsidering the move.
Zelensky urges Trump to get China to help end Russia's invasion
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky says he asked Donald Trump to press China's Xi Jinping to use Beijing's influence over Moscow and end the war on his country.
Zelensky told reporters late on Friday that he has not yet received feedback from the White House about Trump's talks with Xi, but expects to learn the outcome.
Nato countries have called China a "decisive enabler" of Russian president Vladimir Putin's invasion.
Zelensky was also in the US this week on a trip coinciding with the UN General Assembly. He met with Trump on Tuesday.
Zelensky met with US senators and Congress members during his trip and said he thanked them for their bipartisan support in passing a powerful sanctions bill aimed at Moscow last month. Trump signed the bill into law last week but hasn't enacted the measures yet.
Inside the real war games as Europe readies for an attack by Russia
As warnings increase about a Russian attack on a Nato country, real-world war-games, are happening all the time. But the real danger is the potential for hysteria, fear and miscalculation to turn a shadow war into something much worse, writes Owen Matthews:
Little movement on Ukraine peace after turbulent week of UN diplomacy
The UN General Assembly concluded on Friday after a week of speeches, meetings and hallway diplomacy.
While they reached no breakthroughs onthe world's most intractable conflicts, talks on the Iran and Ukraine wars inched forward.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio held talks with Russia's foreign minister Sergei Lavrov, after which he said Ukraine and Russia had both voiced an interest in a limited ceasefire involving grain and energy-related targets.
Ukraine and its allies are racing to secure these limited agreements before winter, fearing renewed Russian strikes on power and heating facilities.
But hours after Rubio spoke on Wednesday, Lavrov addressed the Security Council meeting on Ukraine, showing no indication Russia was prepared to engage on any subject. "Europe, whatever it thinks, just wants to get a pause, and it wants to use it to pump the Kyiv regime with weapons," Lavrov said.
UN refugee chief urges Security Council to do more to end wars
The UN's refugee chief used his first speech at the Security Council yesterday to call for a renewed focus on ending conflicts and crises, so that more than 117 million people forced to flee their homes can return and don't spend generations displaced in a foreign country.
The Ukraine war was just one of the conflicts cited by Barham Salih, who told the Council's 15 members that they have "a unique responsibility to help make peace possible."
He said the conflict started by Vladimir Putin's invasion in 2022 had displaced millions inside the country and sent millions more fleeing to other countries.
"For the millions of people forced from their homes - and the millions more who should never have to flee - I urge you to use that responsibility," the former refugee, who was president of Iraq from 2018 to 2022, told the meeting on the sidelines of the annual UN gathering of world leaders.
Drone hits Russia's Ilsky oil refinery
Ukrainian drones reportedly targeted the Ilsky oil refinery in Russia's Krasnodar Krai, causing a fire at the facility.
Local governor Veniamin Kondratiev said that the Ukrainian drones targeted Seversky district, which houses one of the largest oil-processing facilities in southern Russia.
The extent of the damage to the refinery and casualties were not immediately known.
Government warned Homes for Ukraine funding cut may 'send wrong message to Putin'
Planned government cuts to the Homes for Ukraine Scheme could "send the wrong message to Putin" by giving the impression that Western support for Kyiv is faltering, a Conservative former defence secretary has warned.
Starting from 1 January, monthly "thank-you" payments for households hosting Ukrainian refugees are set to drop from £350 to £100.
Local authority funding to support the initiative will also be scaled back on the same date, falling from £5,900 per guest to £3,300 per arrival.
More here.
